_revised: 2026-09-05, same day: the transcription was faithful but the notes were stale. The two color-analysis files contradicted each other, the chino plan prescribed a Western-preppy slim cut that works against the stated goal, and nothing in the folder said what the target register actually is. This file now carries both layers and says which is which: fields marked as facts (size, brands) are still transcription; direction, palette, silhouette, hair and buyNext are a styling judgement made against photographs, and can be argued with.
_excluded: Appearance.md from the same folder is deliberately never transcribed here or anywhere in this repo: it names real people and must never enter a public project.
_undertone: RESOLVED 2026-09-05, by the gold-versus-silver test held at the face: silver clearly better, gold a definite no. That settles Dark Winter and closes the only question this file was carrying. Everything downstream of it was updated in the same pass — the warm neutrals (camel, cream, stone, khaki, chocolate, rust, olive, tan) are out of the palette, out of buyNext, out of the seasonal wardrobe and out of the chino roadmap; the cool accents are promoted from conditional to real. The one non-obvious casualty is the hair note, which had recommended softening the near-black to a warm brown. That recommendation was undertone-dependent and did not survive.
_gaps: The wardrobe direction is written against photographs, not a fitting. Anything about how a specific garment actually falls on him is unverified until something is tried on.

Outfit_Planner.md carried one entry, on Monday: white chunky sweater, 90s light denim, loafers, gold small hoop earrings, trench coat. It is kept here rather than in his planner because the earrings and the chunky-knit-plus-trench combination read as someone else's outfit — possibly Eunice's, possibly saved inspiration. The undertone test adds a small piece of evidence rather than proof: gold at the ear is the metal he just ruled out, and light 90s denim is a warm wash. Nothing is lost; it just should not stand as Philipp's Monday until he confirms it.

Trouser model names shift every season. The chino plan holds the brands and the cut; the specific SKUs in the original note are already partly superseded and should be re-checked in store rather than trusted here.

direction.register: Modern preppy, elevated — mature, not collegiate
direction.thesis: The wardrobe he was already buying toward (Ralph Lauren, Suitsupply, Charles Tyrwhitt) stops being an exception and becomes the actual plan: tailored coats and knitwear over a collared shirt, chinos with a clean line, camel and khaki back in alongside the cool core. Preppy's usual signals — bright polos, popped collars, varsity branding — are exactly the collegiate register this avoids; the 2026 version of this look is described everywhere as sophisticated and mature rather than campus, and that is the half being kept.
direction.builtFrom: Three facts about him, not a look: colouring that is Dark Winter and high-contrast, a 25 cm waist-to-hip drop, and a face that reads a decade younger than the passport. Those decide the trouser cut and how far the styling may mature regardless of register; the palette itself is cool by test, with camel and khaki confirmed back in on his own report on 2026-09-06.
direction.onTheOriginalFraming: This has been rewritten twice, and both edits are worth keeping visible rather than smoothing over. First written in Korean-actor vocabulary because that was asked for, then generalised — the palette, cut and hair never actually depended on the label, only the reference photos did. Then, on 2026-09-06, the register itself changed: from quiet, dark minimalism to modern preppy, and Gong Yoo, Hyun Bin and Park Seo-joon were genuinely accurate references for the old register specifically, not for this one. Gong Yoo got a second look before being dropped: as a person he is described as versatile — suits to streetwear, no preppy label — and the one look with real preppy DNA, the Goblin/Kim Shin cardigan-over-crewneck sweater set, belongs to a wealthy-immortal costume rather than to his own documented style. A fictional character's wardrobe is a thinner basis for a real style reference than an actor's own red-carpet choices, so it didn't survive the fuller look. Two separate corrections, two separate reasons: one about vocabulary, one about which wardrobe was actually wanted.
direction.ageRead: Reads early-to-mid 30s in photographs, not 43: full hairline, even skin tone, no deep static lines. The clothes are currently the oldest thing in the picture. That widens the range rather than narrowing it — the limiter is context (school, parent evenings, Germany), not the birth year, and over-mature styling would hand back years the face has not lost.

notThis.why: Sheer fabric, embellishment, stage pieces — the idol register the Anson Lo photo pointed at. That is stage costume rather than a wardrobe, and it reads as costume in the room where most of these clothes are actually worn.

Bright polos, popped collars, varsity jackets, baseball caps, graphic knitwear — the campus version of this register, and the thing '2026 modern preppy' is explicitly defined against in the coverage that named it. It would read as costume on a 43-year-old for the same reason the idol register would: borrowed youth rather than his own.

direction.referencesNote: Two searches for an adult, non-idol Asian figure specifically labelled 'preppy' came back close to empty — that label attaches almost mostly to K-pop idols doing the collegiate version. Byeon Woo Seok is the one exception actually sourced for it. Beckham and Reynolds are who the same coverage names when it isn't restricted to Asian figures at all — both are repeatedly cited by name for exactly this register, mature and tailored rather than campus. Neither shares his colouring or build, but the palette is already settled from his own colouring and the metal/fabric test, not from a reference photo, so that stopped being the job a reference had to do. What they're for now is silhouette and attitude only: tailored-but-relaxed, not costume, not campus.

references.name: Byeon Woo Seok
references.why: Actor, not idol; Prada ambassador; documented in cable-knit-over-collared-shirt layering — the core preppy combination, executed adult rather than campus. Age and build read close to his own.

references.name: David Beckham
references.why: Named directly in 2026 coverage of the trend: 'blending traditional tailoring with casual, sporty elements'. Mature, not collegiate, and the sportswear-into-tailoring move matches a man who trains regularly.

references.name: Ryan Reynolds
references.why: Named in the same coverage: 'clean, polished ensembles with a touch of whimsy'. The whimsy is the one thing to leave behind — the register wanted here is quieter than his press-tour persona — but the clean, tailored-casual base is exactly it.

direction.readOfCurrentPhotos: Four photographs, four sets of functional clothing: sport tee, polo, sport tee, printed sweatshirt. Not a taste problem — a control problem. Nothing in the set is a chosen silhouette. What already works: the gum-sole Sambas, and navy, which appears in three of four and flatters in all three. What works against him: the printed sweatshirt (busy, boxy, adds volume exactly where the training is removing it) and visible athletic branding outside the gym.

hair.priority: The single biggest lever — roughly 60% of the effect is decided before any garment is chosen. Hair either rounds the face or lengthens it, and nothing worn below the collar can undo that.
hair.current: Short, flat on top, growing forward, no taper at the sides and no volume at the crown. It rounds the face and takes height away.
hair.cut: Two-block — 7–10 cm on top, sides tapered rather than shaved. If the name does not land at the barber, ask for length and volume on top with the sides tapered short but not clipped.
hair.shape: Soft side sweep or a loose middle part, with lift at the crown
hair.color: Leave it. Near-black is a Dark Winter's own colour and the high contrast against the skin is the asset. If it is ever touched, a cool dark brown — ash or espresso, never caramel or warm brown.
hair.product: Matte clay, not gel. Blow-dry lift from underneath first — glossy is a decade out of date.
hair.why: Vertical lift lengthens the face and gives the jaw its line back; shaved sides would read harder than intended and add years the face has not earned. The colour advice here used to say the opposite — soften the black to a warm brown — and the undertone test overturned it. That recommendation was warm-season reasoning applied to cool skin, and it was the one thing in this file genuinely riding on the answer. The cut is unaffected: it comes from face shape, not colouring.

palette.confidence: Settled for metal, not for every fabric. Depth and contrast were never in doubt. The gold-versus-silver test (2026-09-05) is the strongest-supported claim in here for metal specifically — reflective gold at the jaw is a definite no, silver reads clean — and that rule is not in question. What was overreached was extending it to every warm-toned fabric: on 2026-09-06 he reported his own camel coat and khaki both suit him, which a metal test cannot actually rule out. A polished gold ring returns raw, saturated warmth straight onto the skin; a matte wool coat is muted and sits further from the face, and depth/muting can outweigh hue in a way a mirror shows and a metal swatch cannot. So: metal is a closed question, cool only. Fabric neutrals are open beyond the deep core — camel and khaki are back in, on his word, and nothing else warm has been tested.
palette.established: Near-black hair, dark brown eyes, light-to-medium skin, high hair-to-skin contrast. Deep colours hold across every lighting seen so far — black and navy both sit at the face without draining it.
palette.resolved: Cool for metal: silver at the face reads clean, gold pulls yellow into the skin. Dark Winter depth and contrast stand regardless. Fabric is less absolute than metal — see `warmNeutrals` below for the two colours his own mirror has already settled.
palette.rule: Deep tones throughout, and let the contrast stand. Black is a real neutral here, mid tones are not. Charcoal and true white are the cool default; camel and khaki are allowed too, on his own report — see `warmNeutrals`.
palette.metal: Silver, steel, white gold, gunmetal. This is the direct output of the test rather than a separate opinion, and it is the cheapest rule in the file to follow: watch, belt buckle, glasses frames, any ring. Gold sits at the wrist and the face, which is exactly where a wrong metal shows. This rule is about metal only — it does not extend to camel or khaki fabric, see `warmNeutrals`.

accent.note: Unlocked by the test. These were the cool half of the old conditional block; they are now simply part of the palette, and they are where colour is allowed to happen in an otherwise very dark wardrobe.

warmNeutrals.note: Reopened 2026-09-06. The metal test ruled out gold and, by extrapolation, every warm-toned fabric — but a fabric was never actually tested, and he reported that his own camel coat and khaki both suit him. Metal stays cool-only, settled; these two are back on his word, not on a retest. Nothing else warm has been asked about — this is a two-item list, not a reopening of the whole ruled-out group.

looks.note: Added 2026-09-05 because the page could describe a wardrobe but not show one. Every colour here comes from `palette.core` or `palette.accent` — these are assemblies, not new decisions, and if the palette changes these have to change with it. Five is deliberate: enough to cover the week he actually has, few enough that each one is a real outfit rather than a combination generator.

imageStyle.adaptedFrom: The Teaching Hub house style — 'black and white graphic novel illustration, bold clean ink lines, no grey gradients, white background, no text, no labels, no captions'. Reused so the two projects look like they come from the same hand.
imageStyle.deviation: One deliberate change: colour is allowed. On a wardrobe page the colour IS the content — a navy knit under a charcoal overshirt is the whole point — and a black-and-white plate would remove exactly the thing the reader came for. So: ink linework as in Teaching Hub, but garments filled flat in the palette hexes, with no rendering, no gradients and no fabric texture.

correction.problem: The first two renders (school-day, parent-evening) came back reading as modern preppy / dark academia — glossy K-webtoon shading and doe-eyed rendering rather than the graphic-novel ink asked for, a flapped topstitched chest pocket, a button-down collar, and trousers with a visible break at the shoe. None of that was written into the prompt; the generator defaulted to the dominant house style for 'handsome young Asian man' illustrations, which is exactly that look. The palette and garments were correct — the rendering and a few unstated details were not.
correction.fix: prefix and figure below now say explicitly what they used to leave to chance: matte flat ink, no glossy or anime/webtoon shading, no doe-eyed romance-comic rendering, matte textured hair rather than a glossy side part, no decorative top-stitching or flapped pockets, no crease-break at the shoe. The parent-evening shirt keeps its collar — a plain spread collar is exactly right under an open coat — but loses the button-down oxford collar (the version with buttons at the points), which is the specific detail that read Ivy. This is not a new direction — it is the one already written in `direction` and `hair`, enforced in the prompt instead of assumed.
correction.existingImages: school-day.png and parent-evening.png predate this fix and were not regenerated — that is a real cost, not a rounding error, and worth redoing only if the drift bothers him enough to spend the effort again.

imageStyle.prefix: Full-length fashion-plate illustration in a graphic novel style — flat matte ink, like a European or American adult graphic novel, not an anime or webtoon romance comic. Bold clean black ink outlines of even weight, no cross-hatching, no soft cel-shading, no grey gradients, no glossy highlights anywhere including on hair and skin. Garments filled with flat solid colour exactly as specified, no texture and no fabric rendering. Plain white background, no scenery, no props, no shadow on the ground. No text, no labels, no captions, no logos, no visible branding, no decorative top-stitching, no flapped or patterned pockets — keep every garment plain and unornamented.
imageStyle.figure: The same man in all five images so they read as one series: early-30s East Asian man, slim athletic build, mature and quiet rather than boyish or doe-eyed, calm neutral expression with no smile. Near-black hair with length and volume on top and tapered sides, matte and textured with natural separation — not glossy, not a slicked or glassy side part. Standing straight and facing the viewer, arms relaxed at his sides, full body visible from head to shoes. Trousers fall in one continuous straight line with no crease and no break at the shoe.
imageStyle.suffix: Portrait orientation, roughly 3:4. The whole figure must fit inside the frame with clear margin above the head and below the shoes.
imageStyle.howToUse: Concatenate prefix + figure + the look's own `imagePrompt` + suffix, generate, and drop the file into hub/style/img/ named after the occasion slug — school-day.png, parent-evening.png, weekend.png, evening-out.png, colour-carefully.png. The build picks it up on the next run and replaces the drawn placeholder; .png, .jpg and .webp are all accepted.
imageStyle.background: A transparent background is better than white if the generator can do it, because the page has a dark theme as well as a light one. If it cannot, white is fine — the build puts the image on its own white plate so it looks deliberate in both themes rather than like a bug.

rules.why: Hip 105 cm over waist 80 cm is a 25 cm drop. A slim cut pulls at the seat and advertises exactly the ratio the training is working on; straight falls clear of the hip and lengthens the leg.
The taper is being built in the gym. Outerwear with a real shoulder seam — overshirt, coat, unstructured blazer — anticipates it instead of waiting for it.
One depth of colour head to foot reads as height. Splitting light-over-dark cuts the body in half at the waist, which is the one place not to draw a line.
A long unbroken vertical is the most reliable lengthening device there is. Double-breasted adds width across the chest and works against it.

rules.rule: No visible branding outside the gym
rules.why: Sport logos say 'on the way to train'. The clothes should not be doing that when the destination is a classroom.

rules.rule: Relaxed, never skinny — and never baggy
rules.why: Easy through the leg, clean at the line. Tight reads dated and fights the hip; oversized reads borrowed and loses the shoulder the whole silhouette is built on.

seasonalWardrobe.note: Rewritten 2026-09-05 into the target register, then corrected the same day when the undertone test came back cool — cream, stone, camel, chocolate, tortoise and dark brown all removed. The four-season structure, the straight-leg correction and the tonal-column rule are unchanged throughout.
seasonalWardrobe.styleNote: Natural fabrics — wool, cotton, leather. The rule that carries every season: one depth of colour throughout, a defined shoulder on whatever is outermost. Neutrals default cool — charcoal and true white — with camel and khaki confirmed as the two exceptions.

chinoPlan.goal: End goal: capsule wardrobe largely in Ralph Lauren. This used to be framed as a collector's habit tolerated despite the styling, back when the register was quiet minimalism. Under modern preppy it is the opposite — Ralph Lauren is close to the definitive brand for this register, so wanting it and the styling actually agreeing is the correction, not a coincidence.
chinoPlan.midGoal: Interim: a pragmatic mix — Dockers (budget), Suitsupply (midrange), Ralph Lauren (premium)
chinoPlan.fit: Straight leg, mid-to-high rise. Ask for the straight or relaxed cut by fit, not by model name.

revision.change: Fit corrected from Slim Fit + Mid-Rise to Straight + Mid-High-Rise, 2026-09-05. Colours followed the metal test the same day — stone and Classic Khaki out — then Khaki came back in on 2026-09-06 when he confirmed it suits him; stone stays out, untested. Brands and the Ralph Lauren end goal stand throughout.
revision.why: The fit change rests on a measurement — a 25 cm waist-to-hip drop, where a slim cut pulls at the seat and shortens the leg line — and stands regardless of colour. The colour history is worth keeping honest: the gold-versus-silver test ruled out gold jewellery, and that got extended to every warm fabric including Ralph Lauren's own Classic Khaki, the reason half their catalogue looks the way it does. That extension didn't survive contact with his own coat and his own trousers. Khaki chino is back; stone remains untested and stays out until it is.
